spawn · trust experience

Two nouns, three verbs,
one number.

Underneath: an endorsement mesh with five proven properties, twelve red-team findings, a passkey-sealed root, and committed-SAS ceremonies. On screen: devices and hosts, which you approve, possess, and remove — plus one six-digit number when trust is created, and the passkey you already know from everywhere else. Nothing was weakened to get there; it was hidden behind the only check a human is actually good at.

The mental model

Everything a user ever needs to know

Three sentences. Every screen is one of them happening — no screen is anything else.

1

Approve a device once — type one number — and it can reach every host.

2

Remove a device and it loses access everywhere, instantly and forever.

3

Your passkey brings everything back, even if you lose every device.

The concept budget

Six concepts, one borrowed

Every screen is built from these and nothing else. The protocol's own vocabulary — root, chain, anchor, pin, bundle, heal, endorsement, SAS, fingerprint, key, revoke — never appears. Neither does "recovery": the passkey is borrowed vocabulary, never taught, and it carries the entire root lifecycle silently.

device — the phone or laptop in your hand host — what your agents run on; the app's own name for them approve — admit a device already on the list possess — attach a host; the terminal's own verb remove — revoke, forever passkey — borrowed from the platform; silently the whole safety net the number — the one human check

The screens

One destination, two ceremonies, one refusal

Every state below shipped only after being rendered, screenshotted, and re-worked until it looked deliberate — desktop and mobile.

Access — the one destination

One screen, named for what it governs rather than one of its row types: devices, hosts, and the last three trust events. Each row says who vouched for it and when — the audit trail lives in the rows, not in a security console. Right: no-passkey mode is just the same screen with an amber strip stating its one real cost.

Approve a device

A device is on the list the moment it signs in — approval is the transition, not an insertion. The new device shows the six digits; the trusted device types them, because entering is the check and can't be waved through. With a passkey none of these screens exist — signing in is the approval, and recovery after total loss is the same non-flow.

Possess a host

One command in the host's terminal — the product's own verb, printed by the product itself — then the identical number check: the terminal prints the digits, the device confirms them. The same ceremony component serves both flows; a user who has linked a phone already knows how to possess a server.

The number check — every remaining state

The machinery before the number is one spinner. A mismatch is terminal: red, final, no "approve anyway" — the protocol's one human comparison is not softenable, so the UI doesn't offer to.

Remove a device

Revocation in one breath: instant, everywhere, permanent, and the way back is a fresh link — never an undo. If a host trusts only this device, the dialog names it and steers to recovery first; with recovery on, a passkey touch keeps the host reachable through the removal.

Connection refused

A refused device gets its exact next step, never a raw error. A removed device is told when and by whom it was removed — the audit surface at its sharpest — and offered the only honest path back: starting over as a new device.

History

The full trust log, one plain sentence per event, newest first. This is how a compromised device's rogue link is noticed — and the header says exactly what to do about a surprise.

Desktop

The same components in an app window: the roster as a settings pane with the row menu open (Rename / Remove — everything a row can do), confirms sitting over the dimmed page so their consequences read in context, and an approval request arriving as a corner toast over whatever you were doing. Ceremonies keep their focused card at every size.

Mobile

The same screens at 390px — nothing cracks, nothing hides.

The deleted-complexity ledger

What a naive design shows — and this one doesn't

Simplicity here is subtraction with receipts: each row names the invariant that lets the thing disappear.

A naive design showsThis design showsWhy nothing breaks
Hex key fingerprints to eyeball Nothing The committed six-digit check is stronger than fingerprint eyeballing and is the only comparison on modern endpoints; older hosts fall back to the full fingerprint, never a weaker code A5
Endorsements as inspectable objects "Linked by MacBook Pro · Jun 3" on the row Signatures are machine-verified; humans only ever needed who and when — which is exactly the detection requirement P2 · R4
The trust graph and its chains A flat list The mesh is proven complete, so "linked" is a truthful single state; chains are transport, not status P1
Root status, heal progress, re-anchoring events "Signed in with passkey" as provenance Healing is machine work authorized by the passkey; there is no decision a user could make better than the protocol P4 · §4.1
A device-by-host permission matrix Nothing Every device reaches every host — the matrix would be an N×M grid of identical checkmarks P1
Pairing modes and fallback choices One number check The rollout rule already picks the stronger check automatically; the UI never offers the choice App. A
A revocation list to manage Remove, plus one sentence in its dialog "Instantly and permanently, everywhere" is the entire truth of the add-only deny-list P3
"Un-remove" for second thoughts "Approve it as a new device" Tombstones are permanent; re-admission is a fresh ceremony — one number, so forgiveness stays cheap R10
A passkey / no-passkey mode switch Nothing — having a passkey is the mode The mode is a consequence, not a setting; its cost is stated where it's decided and again where it bites R8
Ceremony internals: commit, reveal, nonces "Securing the connection…" The ceremony's soundness never depended on the user watching it happen A5
A recovery wizard Nothing — signing in with the passkey restores everything Unlock triggers the heal; the best disaster flow is the one users already know §4.1
Key-rotation UI after reset "Rebuilds the next time you use a passkey" The successor root is minted automatically at unlock; the old one stays dead §4.1 · R10

The flows

Human cost, counted

First device, first host

Sign up → run one command → type one number

The first device needs no ceremony — there is nothing to approve from yet. Total human cost of a working setup: one number.

New device, with passkey

Sign in → touch passkey → done

Zero trust screens. Recovery after losing everything is intentionally this same non-flow.

New device, no passkey

Sign in → appear as waiting → a trusted device types the number

One check admits the device to every host, present and future.

Remove a device

Overflow → Remove → confirm

Effective mid-session: the removed device's screens drop and it lands on its "removed" page, told who removed it.

Passkey lifecycle

Account settings → add or remove

Managed with the account, like every product's passkeys. Adding one mints the safety net; rotation is automatic at the next passkey sign-in.

Refused connection

Blocked screen → exact next step

Removed and not-yet-approved devices each get one honest path forward — never a raw error.

Nothing weakened

Where each protocol guarantee lives on screen

The human number match (A5)

Kept in both ceremonies as entry, not tap-to-approve: one side shows the number, the other types it. One shared component; mismatch is terminal with no override path.

Revocation: instant, total, permanent (P3 · R1 · R10)

"Instantly and permanently" in the dialog; live sessions drop; the only way back is a fresh approval.

Audited visibility (R4)

Provenance on every row, the History log, and the removed screen naming its remover.

The stranded-host hazard (R5)

The remove dialog names the hosts at risk and steers to a passkey first — warn, never silently strand.

No-passkey mode (R8)

Fully supported: it is simply not having a passkey. The cost is stated in one dismissible nudge and restated where it bites.

Honest claims (P2 · P3′)

The roster says "only you can approve one" — approval is the single door, and denial is the only power the server keeps.
